questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: E.1 (Structure of the atom), E.2 (Quantum physics)
questions.topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
questions.subtopic: E.1 / E.2 Photons, the photoelectric effect and matter waves
questions.challenge_mechanism: Three of the five items turn on a unit rather than an idea: nanometres against metres, electron-volts against joules, and the factor of two inside the kinetic energy expression, so a student who knows the physics but loses the unit loses the mark.
questions.question: Each question below is self-contained. Take the Planck constant as $6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s, the speed of light in vacuum as $3.00\times10^{8}$ m per second, the elementary charge as $1.60\times10^{-19}$ C, the electron mass as $9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg, and $1\,\mathrm{eV}=1.60\times10^{-19}$ J.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Light of wavelength 420 nm is incident on a metal surface in a darkened room. What is the energy carried by a single photon of this light, and what is that energy when it is expressed in electron-volts rather than in joules?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Photon energy is $hc/\lambda$, with the wavelength converted from nanometres to metres before dividing.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the correct numerical value in electron-volts, quoted with the wrong unit; it is $2.96$ eV, not $2.96$ J.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Uses $E=hc\lambda$, multiplying by the wavelength instead of dividing by it.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the frequency in hertz; the photon energy still has to be found by multiplying by the Planck constant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A metal has a work function of $2.28$ eV. Light of frequency $8.00\times10^{14}$ Hz is shone on it. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The photon energy is $5.30\times10^{-19}$ J or $3.315$ eV, and subtracting the work function leaves $1.035$ eV, which is $1.66\times10^{-19}$ J.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Subtracts $2.28\times10^{-19}$ J rather than converting the work function; $2.28$ eV is $3.65\times10^{-19}$ J.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Adds the work function to the photon energy instead of subtracting it; the work function is the energy that must be paid to escape.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the photon energy itself; the question asks for what remains after the electron has escaped.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For the metal and the illumination described in the previous question, what stopping potential would be measured?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The stopping potential in volts is numerically equal to the maximum kinetic energy in electron-volts, $1.035$ eV.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the work function in electron-volts, which sets the threshold, not the stopping potential for this frequency.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is the photon energy in electron-volts before the work function has been subtracted.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Emission does occur here because the photon energy exceeds the work function, so the stopping potential is not zero.

parts.label: d
parts.text: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of $150$ V. What is its de Broglie wavelength?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The kinetic energy is $eV$, so the momentum is the square root of $2\,m\,e\,V$, and the wavelength is $h$ divided by that momentum.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Omits the factor of two and uses the square root of $m\,e\,V$ for the momentum.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Uses the proton mass in place of the electron mass, which shortens the wavelength by the square root of the mass ratio.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Treats the accelerating potential as $150$ kV rather than $150$ V.

parts.label: e
parts.text: A laser emits $2.0$ mW of light at a wavelength of $640$ nm. How many photons does it emit each second?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Each photon carries $hc/\lambda=3.11\times10^{-19}$ J, and dividing the power by that energy gives the emission rate.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Reads the wavelength as $640$ micrometres rather than nanometres, making each photon a thousand times less energetic.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Multiplies the photon count by the elementary charge, which converts joules to electron-volts and has no place in a count.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the energy of one photon in joules; the question asks for the number emitted per second.

questions.answer:
**(a)** $E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{420\times10^{-9}}=4.74\times10^{-19}$ J, which is option A. **(A1)** Option B is the same number in electron-volts, so it catches anyone who converts and then forgets which unit they are in; option C comes from multiplying by the wavelength; option D is the frequency, one step short. **(a)** A

**(b)** $hf=6.63\times10^{-34}\times8.00\times10^{14}=5.304\times10^{-19}$ J $=3.315$ eV. Subtracting the work function gives $K_{\max}=3.315-2.28=1.035$ eV $=1.66\times10^{-19}$ J, option A. **(A1)** The trap in option B is subtracting $2.28\times10^{-19}$ J, which is not the same quantity as $2.28$ eV. **(b)** A

**(c)** $eV_s=K_{\max}$ in electron-volts, so $V_s=1.035$ V, option A. **(A1)** The rule is that one electron-volt corresponds to one volt for a singly charged particle, which is why the conversion is trivial once (b) is in eV and impossible if it is left in joules. **(c)** A

**(d)** $p=\sqrt{2\,m\,eV}=\sqrt{2\times9.11\times10^{-31}\times1.60\times10^{-19}\times150}=6.61\times10^{-24}$ kg m per second, so $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{p}=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{6.61\times10^{-24}}=1.00\times10^{-10}$ m, option A. **(A1)** The factor of two is the discriminator here, and it is worth noting that $0.10$ nm is of the order of an atomic spacing, which is why electron diffraction works. **(d)** A

**(e)** $E=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{640\times10^{-9}}=3.11\times10^{-19}$ J, so the rate is $\dfrac{2.0\times10^{-3}}{3.11\times10^{-19}}=6.4\times10^{15}$ per second, option A. **(A1)** Option B is the most dangerous distractor in the cluster because the arithmetic is identical and only the prefix differs. **(e)** A
questions.markscheme_notes: One mark per item and there is no negative marking, so a candidate should be advised to commit to an answer rather than leave a blank. In (a) condone $4.7$ to $4.8\times10^{-19}$ J. In (b) allow the answer in eV provided it is identified as such, and note that a candidate who works entirely in joules must convert the work function first; that conversion is where the mark is actually won or lost. In (d) allow $0.10$ nm or $1.0\times10^{-10}$ m, and credit a candidate who reaches $1.42\times10^{-10}$ m only if they show the factor of two explicitly, since otherwise the working is wrong even though the answer looks close. In (e) accept $6.4\times10^{15}$ to $6.5\times10^{15}$. It is worth telling candidates explicitly that the electron-volt is doing real work in this cluster rather than being decoration: in (b) the subtraction is only possible after the work function has been brought into the same unit as the photon energy, and in (c) the answer in volts is the answer in electron-volts, which is the sense in which the unit simplifies rather than complicates the arithmetic.
questions.explanation: The cluster is deliberately built so that four of the five items are won or lost on a conversion rather than on an idea. Every candidate can state that $E=hf$ and that $K_{\max}=hf-\phi$; far fewer can hold onto the units while doing it, and the distractors are engineered so that each wrong option is a specific, nameable slip — quoting electron-volts as joules, subtracting $2.28\times10^{-19}$ J as though it were $2.28$ eV, dropping the factor of two in $p=\sqrt{2meV}$, reading nanometres as micrometres. This matters beyond the marks: in the examined practical work the same conversions recur constantly, and a student who loses them here will lose them when they are carrying three other uncertainties at the same time. A guessing candidate is unlikely to land on the key in more than one of these, because the wrong options are not random numbers but the results of real errors, which is the design target for a Paper 1A cluster. A useful post-mortem is to ask the class which of the four distractors they actually chose. The distribution is informative: the micrometre slip in (e) and the dropped factor of two in (d) are both errors of attention rather than of understanding, and they respond to a checklist, whereas the electron-volt slips in (a) and (b) usually indicate that the student has not yet internalised what the unit means and needs the conversion written out in full until it becomes automatic.

provenance.adaptation: Original cluster. Wavelengths, work function, accelerating potential and laser power chosen so that each of the four intended slips produces a distinct value that appears among the options, and no two distractors collide.

verification.method: Every key and every distractor recomputed independently in Python to full precision, each distractor confirmed to be the exact result of the named error rather than an arbitrary nearby value.
solution_skeleton: convert the given quantity to SI before substituting
select the photon or matter-wave relation that applies
carry the unit through the conversion to joules or electron-volts
match the value to an option and check the order of magnitude

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.subtopic: A.3 Work done by a varying force, found from the area under a force-extension graph
questions.challenge_mechanism: The data look as though they ought to obey Hooke's law, so the student has to test that assumption from the pattern of first differences before choosing a method, and then has to find the work by numerical integration because no formula applies.

stimulus.title: Student investigation: a non-linear spring
stimulus.body: A student investigates a short steel spring using a force sensor and a metre ruler. The spring is stretched horizontally and the force needed to hold it at a given extension is recorded. The force sensor reads to the nearest 0.05 N and the ruler to the nearest millimetre. The readings are given below. The student intends to use the spring to launch a 0.250 kg trolley along a horizontal track.

table.caption: Force required to hold the spring at a given extension

questions.question: The readings are shown in the table. Answer all parts with reference to the data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State, using evidence from the table, whether the spring obeys Hooke's law over this range.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the work done in extending the spring from zero to $0.120$ m by dividing the area under the force-extension graph into trapezia.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student assumes Hooke's law and uses $W=\tfrac12 kx^2$ with $k$ taken from the reading at $0.120$ m. Calculate the value this gives, and the percentage difference from your answer to (b).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Hence calculate the speed at which the trolley would leave the spring, assuming all of the stored energy is transferred to the trolley, and estimate the percentage uncertainty in this speed from the resolution of the force sensor.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Evaluate whether the trapezium method overestimates or underestimates the true work done, and state why.

questions.answer:
**(a)** It does not. **(A1)** The first differences of the force column are $1.60,\,1.70,\,1.80,\,1.90,\,2.10,\,2.30$ N for equal extension steps of $0.020$ m; they are not constant, and they increase, so the ratio $F/x$ is not constant either and Hooke's law does not hold. **(A1)**

**(b)** Dividing the range into six trapezia of width $0.020$ m,

$$W=0.020\left[\frac{0.00+11.40}{2}+1.60+3.30+5.10+7.00+9.10\right]$$

$$=0.020\left[5.70+26.10\right]=0.020\times31.80=0.636\text{ J}.$$

**(M1)(A1)(A1)** Award the unit mark separately. **(A1)**

**(c)** $k=\dfrac{11.40}{0.120}=95.0$ N per metre, so $W=\tfrac12\times95.0\times0.120^{2}=0.684$ J. **(M1)(A1)** The difference from (b) is $0.684-0.636=0.048$ J, which is $\dfrac{0.048}{0.636}\times100=7.5\%$. **(A1)**

**(d)** $\tfrac12\times0.250\,v^{2}=0.636$, so $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\times0.636}{0.250}}=2.26$ m per second. **(M1)(A1)** Each of the six interior force readings carries an uncertainty of $0.05$ N, so the worst-case uncertainty in the sum is $0.020\times6\times0.05=0.006$ J, which is $0.9\%$ of $0.636$ J. **(M1)** Since $v$ depends on the square root of the energy, the percentage uncertainty in the speed is half of this, about $0.5\%$. **(A1)**

**(e)** It overestimates. **(A1)** The force-extension graph is curving upwards, so each straight-line chord lies above the curve between the two readings, and the trapezia include a little area that is not under the curve at all. **(A1)** Two refinements are worth recording. The trapezium estimate could be improved by halving the interval width, which would require readings at 0.010 m intervals and would roughly quarter the method error, since the error of the composite rule falls as the square of the step; a candidate who suggests this has understood that the limitation is the sampling and not the arithmetic. Alternatively Simpson's rule would be exact here for a quadratic force law and would remove the curvature bias altogether, though it needs an odd number of intervals and so cannot be applied to this table without an extra reading. The reason the simple approach is adequate is that the method error is far below the uncertainty contributed by the force sensor, so refining the integration before improving the sensor would be wasted effort.
questions.markscheme_notes: In (a) the evidence must be numerical; a statement that the graph is not a straight line through the origin earns the mark only if a pair of ratios or differences is quoted. In (b) allow $0.63$ to $0.64$ J and accept an equivalent count of squares if the working is shown; the method mark is for the trapezium sum, not for the answer. In (c) allow $7.4\%$ to $7.6\%$ and allow the difference to be expressed against either value provided it is stated which. In (d) allow $2.25$ to $2.27$ m per second, and note that the halving of the percentage uncertainty is the point of the part: a candidate who quotes $0.9\%$ for the speed has not applied the square root. Allow follow-through from (b). In (e) the reason must refer to the curvature of the graph; 'the trapezia are not exact' is not sufficient. Note also that the first and last ordinates carry half weight in the trapezium sum, and candidates frequently give them full weight; that error alone changes the answer by about five per cent and should be looked for specifically. Where a candidate uses a counting-squares method instead, credit it on the same terms, but require the scale of one square to be stated in joules before the count is accepted. In (e) accept an answer based on a sketch if the chord and the curve are both drawn and the area between them is identified.
questions.explanation: The item exists because the obvious formula is the wrong one and the data hide that fact. Every textbook spring question uses $\tfrac12kx^{2}$, and the table has been constructed so that this gives a plausible-looking $0.684$ J against the correct $0.636$ J — a $7.5\%$ error, large enough to matter and small enough that no candidate will spot it by eye. The only way to see it is to look at the first differences, which is why (a) is worth two marks and comes first: it forces the test before the method is chosen. Part (b) then requires numerical integration, which is a skill the examined practical work demands and which most candidates have met only in passing. Part (d) contains a second, quieter trap: the percentage uncertainty in the speed is half that in the energy, because of the square root, and a candidate who propagates it directly has missed the relationship between the two. Part (e) closes the loop by asking about the sign of the method error, and the answer follows from the same curvature that made Hooke's law fail in the first place. The item also carries a lesson about when to stop refining a measurement. The method error in the trapezium rule here is a fraction of a per cent while the sensor contributes about one per cent, so the sensible next investment is a better force sensor, not a finer integration rule; candidates rarely say this, and it is worth drawing out because the same judgement recurs in every experiment they will meet.

provenance.adaptation: Original dataset, generated so that the first differences increase smoothly, the trapezium and Hookean answers differ by about 7.5%, and the force-sensor resolution gives a clean 0.9% uncertainty in the work.

verification.method: Trapezium sum recomputed in Python; first differences checked to be strictly increasing; the Hookean estimate, the percentage difference, the launch speed and the uncertainty propagation all recomputed independently.
solution_skeleton: test the assumed model using first differences of the table
replace the closed-form integral with a numerical one over the tabulated data
quantify the error the wrong model would have introduced
convert the stored energy to a speed and propagate the uncertainty through the square root
judge the sign of the numerical method error from the curvature

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.subtopic: B.3 Testing the ideal gas equation against data; uncertainty and systematic error
questions.challenge_mechanism: Nothing is plotted and nothing is linearised; the student has to form the invariant directly from the table, propagate three instrument uncertainties into it, and then decide whether one row is genuinely anomalous or merely imprecise.

stimulus.title: Student investigation: testing the ideal gas equation
stimulus.body: A student traps a fixed amount of gas in a sealed syringe connected to a pressure gauge and placed in a water bath. The pressure, the volume and the temperature of the water bath are recorded for six different settings. The pressure gauge reads to the nearest 1 kPa, the syringe scale to the nearest 1 cubic centimetre, and the thermometer to the nearest 0.5 K. The student wants to know whether the data support the ideal gas equation, and to determine the amount of gas in the syringe.

questions.question: The readings are shown in the table. Take the molar gas constant as $8.31$ J per mole per kelvin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of $\dfrac{pV}{T}$ for each of the six settings, stating the unit, and hence determine the amount of gas in the syringe in moles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the percentage uncertainty in $\dfrac{pV}{T}$ for the first row of the table, using the resolutions given in the method.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify which row is not consistent with the other five, and state the temperature that would bring it into line with them.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest a physical cause for the inconsistency, and describe a change to the experimental method that would remove it.

questions.answer:
**(a)** With $p$ in kPa and $V$ in cubic centimetres, $pV$ is in units of $10^{3}\times10^{-6}=10^{-3}$ J, so the unit of $\dfrac{pV}{T}$ is $10^{-3}$ J per kelvin. The six values are:

$$166.3,\;166.1,\;166.4,\;166.2,\;166.3,\;161.2\quad(10^{-3}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}).$$

**(M1)(A1)** Excluding the last row, the mean is $166.3\times10^{-3}$ J per kelvin. Since $\dfrac{pV}{T}=nR$, the amount of gas is

$$n=\frac{166.3\times10^{-3}}{8.31}=2.00\times10^{-2}\text{ mol}.$$

**(M1)(A1)**

**(b)** For the first row, the fractional uncertainties are $\dfrac{1}{100}=1.0\%$ in the pressure, $\dfrac{1}{499}=0.20\%$ in the volume and $\dfrac{0.5}{300}=0.17\%$ in the temperature. **(M1)(A1)** Adding these in quadrature,

$$\sqrt{1.0^{2}+0.20^{2}+0.17^{2}}=\sqrt{1.00+0.040+0.029}=1.0\%.$$

**(A1)**

**(c)** The last row is the outlier: its value of $161.2\times10^{-3}$ J per kelvin lies about $3\%$ below the others, against a measurement uncertainty of about $0.6\%$ for that row, so the discrepancy is several times larger than the uncertainty and cannot be put down to precision. **(M1)(A1)** The temperature that would bring it into line is $T=\dfrac{pV}{nR}=\dfrac{200\times332\times10^{-3}}{8.31\times2.00\times10^{-2}}=399$ K, so about $400$ K rather than $412$ K. **(A1)**

**(d)** The most likely cause is that the thermometer was not measuring the temperature of the gas. **(A1)** If the bulb or probe was resting outside the water bath, in the laboratory air, or in direct sunlight, or was touching the bench, then it reads something other than the gas temperature, and the recorded $412$ K is an over-read of about $12$ K. **(A1)** This is a systematic error, not a random one: it does not average out over repeats, and it grows with the setting, which is exactly what a sunlit probe would do as the water bath is heated. **(A1)** The change to the method is to immerse the temperature probe in the water bath alongside the syringe and allow enough time for thermal equilibrium before each reading, to shield the bath from direct radiation, and to stir the bath so that it is isothermal; a further improvement is to read the temperature with the probe in the bath rather than from a sensor clipped to the outside of the syringe. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: In (a) allow values within one or two units in the last place and accept the unit expressed as kPa cubic centimetres per kelvin, which is equivalent. The amount of gas should be reported as $2.00\times10^{-2}$ mol; allow $0.0200$ to $0.0201$. In (b) allow the uncertainties to be added linearly, giving about $1.4\%$, provided the method is stated; the quadrature answer is $1.0\%$. In (c) the justification must compare the discrepancy with the uncertainty, not merely point at the row that looks different, and the corrected temperature should be $399$ to $400$ K. In (d) credit any physically sensible cause that is consistent with a temperature over-read, but do not credit 'human error' or 'the reading was wrong'; the improvement must address the cause that has been named. A candidate who suggests that the gas leaked should be asked where the gas went, since the syringe is sealed and the other five rows are consistent. A further condonation is worth recording. Some candidates will compute the invariant as $pV$ against $T$ and attempt a gradient through the origin; this is a perfectly good alternative and should be credited in full provided the last row is excluded from the fit and that exclusion is justified, because a best-fit line through all six points is dragged by the outlier and gives an amount of substance about one per cent low. Others will convert volumes to cubic metres at the start; this is more laborious and introduces more rounding, but is not wrong. What should not be credited is a conclusion reached by eye.
questions.explanation: This item is built as a deliberate contrast with the two data-based questions elsewhere in the bank, both of which ask the student to linearise a relationship and take a gradient. Here there is nothing to plot: the invariant $pV/T$ can be formed directly from each row, so the question tests whether a student recognises an invariant when there is no graph to draw, and whether they know what to do with it afterwards. The real discrimination is in (b) and (c) together. Computing the combined uncertainty is routine; the hard step is using it to decide whether the last row is anomalous or merely imprecise, and that decision cannot be made without the number from (b). A candidate who simply says the row looks wrong has skipped the reasoning entirely. Part (d) then asks for a cause that is consistent with the direction of the error, and the answer has to be about the thermometer rather than about the gas, because the five consistent rows show the gas is behaving properly. The pedagogical point worth carrying forward is that a systematic error in one instrument shows up in every derived quantity and does not improve with repetition, which is why the fix is a change of method rather than more readings. There is a second lesson hiding in the table, and it is worth pointing out to a class that has finished. The pressure readings rise in equal steps of 20 kPa, so the experimenter has varied the independent variable uniformly; that is reasonable but not optimal, because the percentage uncertainty in pressure is largest at the low-pressure end, where it is a full one per cent, and smallest at the top, where it is half that. Spacing the settings so that the percentage uncertainty is roughly constant, or simply taking more readings where the uncertainty is worst, would improve the test at no cost. Candidates who have internalised that uncertainties, and not the readings themselves, should drive the design of an experiment will suggest it without being asked, and the suggestion is a reliable marker of the top grade boundary.

provenance.adaptation: Original dataset, generated from the ideal gas equation with n = 0.0200 mol, rounded to the stated instrument resolutions, with a single seeded +12 K temperature offset in the last row chosen to be about three times the combined measurement uncertainty.

verification.method: Values generated from the ideal gas equation with n = 0.0200 mol and rounded to instrument resolution; the invariant, the mean, the derived amount of substance, the combined uncertainty and the corrected temperature all recomputed in Python.
solution_skeleton: form the invariant directly from each row rather than plotting
propagate the three instrument resolutions into the invariant in quadrature
compare the spread of the invariant against that uncertainty to detect an outlier
solve the invariant for the quantity that would restore consistency
attribute the discrepancy to a systematic effect in one instrument and change the method
